entries.summary: Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution.
entries.text: Seven vulnerabilities have been discovered in Ruby’s regular expression engine and in the case conversion of strings. We are aware of PoCs that prove some of them can be used to trigger remote code execution. We have released Ruby 4.0.10, 3.4.13 and 3.3.14 to fix them. We strongly recommend upgrading. CVE identifiers have been requested for these vulnerabilities but have not been assigned yet, so this advisory refers to them by their GitHub Security Advisory (GHSA) identifiers. GHSA-34m4-m9fh-gqp5: Heap buffer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has a one-byte heap-based buffer overflow in the case conversion of strings. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-7x2q-68qv-6p8x: Double free in regular expression compilation Ruby has a double free in its regular expression engine. Compiling a crafted regular expression pattern may allow remote code execution in applications that compile attacker-controlled patterns. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-87fm-7w84-j2px: Integer overflow in case conversion of strings Ruby has an integer overflow in the case conversion of strings, which causes a heap-based buffer overflow. Changing the case of a crafted string may allow remote code execution. We are aware of PoCs that prove this flaw can be used to trigger RCE in some scenarios. GHSA-wpqw-5qxg-m68r:

entries.summary: We have released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13. They fix several bugs in Ruby’s regular expression engine (Onigmo) that GitLab found could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers.
entries.text: We have released Ruby 4.0.9, 3.4.12 and 3.3.13. They fix several bugs in Ruby’s regular expression engine (Onigmo) that GitLab found could be used for remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab published four CVEs for these issues, and the Ruby releases contain the fixes for the underlying bugs in Ruby. Background GitLab compiles regular expressions supplied by its users, such as patterns in CI configuration, with Regexp.new. GitLab found that specially crafted patterns could corrupt memory while Ruby compiles them, and that this could be turned into remote code execution on GitLab servers. GitLab addressed these issues in its own releases by patching the Ruby it ships, and assigned the following CVE identifiers: CVE-2026-89078: Double Free issue in Regular Expression Parser (GitLab 19.4.1) CVE-2026-93577: Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler (GitLab 19.4.1) CVE-2026-97229: Integer Overflow issue in CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler (GitLab 19.4.2) CVE-2026-110264: Integer Overflow issue in Regular Expression Compiler (GitLab 19.5.1) Fixes in Ruby The following table shows the change in Ruby that fixes the bug behind each CVE, and the first release of each series that contains it. entries.summary: We are pleased to announce the release of Ruby 4.1.0-preview1. Ruby 4.1 introduces Ractor local GC, Windows support of YJIT, autoload_relative, and adds many improvements.
entries.text: We are pleased to announce the release of Ruby 4.1.0-preview1. Ruby 4.1 introduces Ractor local GC, Windows support of YJIT, autoload_relative, and adds many improvements. Ractor improvements A lot of work has gone into making Ractors more stable, performant, and usable. These improvements bring Ractor implementation closer to leaving experimental status. The default GC now runs per Ractor: each Ractor collects its own heap on its own thread without stopping the others, and a stop-the-world collection only runs when it is really needed (explicit full GC.start, shareable-object growth, reclaiming dead Ractors’ heaps). Allocation-heavy Ractor programs now scale like forked processes. GC.start(global: false) can be used when multiple Ractors are running to force a Ractor-local GC. By default, GC.start runs a global GC (all Ractors) like before. This can also be triggered with GC.start(global: true). The global keyword argument has no effect when a single Ractor is running. Visible behavior changes: Ractor#value returns the value only once; a second call raises Ractor::Error. GC.disable/GC.enable act as per-Ractor holds on a process-wide switch: one Ractor’s GC.enable no longer overrides another Ractor’s GC.disable. ObjectSpace.each_object enumerates the calling Ractor’s own objects plus other Ractors’ shareable objects (ObjectSpace.dump_all still covers everything).
